name: skeleton
title: Skeleton
description: A placeholder that keeps the layout of the content it stands in for.

files.content:
import { createContext, useCallback, useContext, useEffect, useRef, useState, } from 'react' import type { ReactNode } from 'react' /** * Whether a `Skeleton` above this point is standing in for content. * * This is the whole of React Spectrum's mechanism: its `Skeleton` renders no element at all, it * publishes a context, and the components that can be skeletonised — `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, * `Link`, `StatusLight`, `Badge` and `Meter` — read it and draw themselves as placeholders. A * component that does not read it keeps rendering, which is why the docs can list exactly which * ones are affected. * * **This library's components do not need to read it**, because the shimmer below goes on an * element that wraps the content rather than on each component's own root (see `Skeleton`). The * context stays public anyway, and that is not decoration: it is the only way a *consumer's* own * component — a chart, a monitor tile — can tell that it is inside a placeholder and skip work it * would otherwise do to draw something nobody can see. `Skeleton.stories.tsx` has one. */ const SkeletonContext = createContext(false) /** * Whether the content here is a placeholder. * * ```tsx * function Uptime({percent}: {percent: number}) { * // Nothing under a skeleton is visible, so there is no point measuring a chart into it. * if (useIsSkeleton()) return
* return
{percent}%
* } * ``` */ export function useIsSkeleton(): boolean { return useContext(SkeletonContext) } /** * The shimmer, as one class list. * * A three-stop gradient whose middle band is the highlight, laid out 300% as wide as the box so * that the sweep has somewhere to travel, and never repeated. The stops are at 33% and 66% of the * *gradient*, which is why a box at rest — one with no animation, under reduced motion — shows the * flat `--muted` end of it rather than a band parked in the middle. * * **The highlight is mixed from the base colour rather than picked as a second grey**, the same * move every hover and pressed state in this system makes: `--foreground` inverts with the theme, * so one rule lightens the dark theme's placeholder and darkens the light theme's. 12% is * `TRACK_WASH`'s wash — a step you can see across a card and cannot mistake for a border. * * `[&_*]:invisible` is what makes the content a placeholder. `visibility`, not `display`, because * a skeleton is a promise about *where things will be*: the subtree leaves the picture and the * accessibility tree while its boxes stay exactly where the real content will land, which is the * whole reason the page does not jump when the content arrives. */ const SHIMMER = [ '[&_*]:invisible', 'bg-no-repeat', '[background-image:linear-gradient(to_right,var(--muted)_33%,color-mix(in_oklch,var(--foreground)_12%,var(--muted))_50%,var(--muted)_66%)]', '[background-size:300%_100%]', ].join(' ') /** The sweep takes two seconds, eased at both ends, and never stops. */ const SWEEP_DURATION = 2000 /** * Whether the reader has asked for less motion, read from the media query and watched, so that * turning it on stops a running sweep rather than waiting for the next mount. * * Read in an effect, never during render: this app is server-rendered, where `window` does not * exist, and a preference read at render time would also be a preference that never changes. */ function usePrefersReducedMotion(): boolean { const [reduced, setReduced] = useState(false) useEffect(() => { const query = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)') const update = () => setReduced(query.matches) update() query.addEventListener('change', update) return () => query.removeEventListener('change', update) }, []) return reduced } export interface SkeletonProps { /** * The content being stood in for — mock data inside your real markup, or nothing at all when the * placeholder is a bare box sized by `className`. */ children?: ReactNode /** * Whether the content is still being fetched. `true` by default, because a `Skeleton` that is * not standing in for anything is a blank box; pass `false` and the children render as they are, * with no element of this component's own in the page. */ isLoading?: boolean /** * The placeholder's own box: `h-4 w-40` for a line of text, `size-10 rounded-full` for an * avatar, `h-24` for a chart. A placeholder wrapped *around* content needs none of this — it * takes the content's size — and a bare one is sized entirely from here. */ className?: string } /** * A placeholder that keeps the layout of the content it stands in for. * * ```tsx * // Mock data inside your real component, the way React Spectrum's docs do it: the placeholder is * // laid out by the markup it is standing in for, so the page does not move when it arrives. * * * * Uptime * api-gateway · last 24 hours * * Every monitor answered within its window. * * * * // One line on its own, sized by the caller rather than by content: * * ``` * * **React Spectrum's `Skeleton` renders no element of its own.** It publishes a context and its * own `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, `Link`, `StatusLight`, `Badge` and `Meter` read it and swap * themselves for a shimmering box, so the placeholder is composed of the components' real * shapes. This library has no `Text` and no `Image` — the sheet has no typography component — * and a skeleton cannot be built out of components that are not here. So the shimmer goes on this * element, which wraps the content instead: **the content is hidden but still laid out, so the box * is the size the content really is**, which is the property that matters. What you lose is one * gradient per component and what you gain is that any markup in this library can be skeletonised * without the component opt-in React Spectrum needed. * * The granularity is the caller's. Wrap a whole card and it shimmers as one surface; wrap each line * and each one shimmers on its own, which is how a skeleton screen is normally drawn: * * ```tsx *
* * *
* ``` * * Three things are deliberately *not* left to the caller: * * - **The sweep is synchronised across the page.** The shimmer is a Web Animation rather than a * CSS keyframe, and every skeleton sets its `startTime` to `0` — React Spectrum's own technique. * A CSS animation starts when each element mounts, so two placeholders that appeared a second * apart are visibly out of step, which reads as two things loading rather than one screen. * - **`prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured**, and what is left is a flat placeholder rather than no * placeholder: the state change the reader asked for, minus the movement. * - **The subtree is `inert`.** Nothing inside is visible, so nothing inside may be tabbed to, * clicked or announced — which is also how React Spectrum disables the form components in a * skeleton. There is no separate "disabled inside a skeleton" prop for a consumer to remember. */ export function Skeleton({ children, isLoading = true, className, }: SkeletonProps) { const reducedMotion = usePrefersReducedMotion() const animation = useRef(null) /** * Start the sweep when the box attaches, and leave it alone afterwards. A re-render replaces this * callback's identity, so React calls it again with the same element — which must not restart the * animation, and does not: it only runs when there is no animation yet. */ const shimmer = useCallback( (element: HTMLDivElement | null) => { const shouldAnimate = isLoading && !reducedMotion if ( shouldAnimate && !animation.current && element && typeof element.animate === 'function' ) { // `startTime` 0 rather than "now": every skeleton on the page is then at the same point in // the same sweep, so the whole screen pulses as one surface. animation.current = element.animate( [{ backgroundPosition: '100%' }, { backgroundPosition: '0%' }], { duration: SWEEP_DURATION, iterations: Infinity, easing: 'ease-in-out', }, ) animation.current.startTime = 0 } else if (!shouldAnimate && animation.current) { animation.current.cancel() animation.current = null } }, [isLoading, reducedMotion], ) useEffect( () => () => { animation.current?.cancel() animation.current = null }, [], ) if (!isLoading) { return ( {children} ) } return (
{children}
) }

A placeholder that keeps the layout of the content it stands in for. ```tsx Uptime api-gateway · last 24 hours Every monitor answered inside its window. ``` | Prop | Type | Default | What it is | | ----------- | ----------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `children` | `ReactNode` | — | the content being stood in for. With none, the placeholder is a box. | | `isLoading` | `boolean` | `true` | `false` renders the children as they are, with no element of its own. | | `className` | `string` | — | the placeholder's own box: `h-4 w-40`, `size-10 rounded-full`, `h-24`. | ## How React Spectrum's works, and what had to change here React Spectrum's `Skeleton` **renders no element at all**. It publishes a context — `SkeletonContext` and `useIsSkeleton` — and the components that can be skeletonised read it and draw themselves as shimmering boxes: `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, `Link`, `StatusLight`, `Badge` and `Meter`. Form components inside one are disabled. So the placeholder is composed of the components' real shapes, and the docs can list exactly which components are affected — which is also the catch: a component that does not read the context keeps rendering as itself. Its shimmer is one class, `loadingStyle`: a three-stop gradient 300% as wide as the box, plus `* { visibility: hidden }`. The sweep is a Web Animation rather than a CSS keyframe, so that every skeleton on the page can be given `startTime = 0` and share one phase, and it is not created at all under `prefers-reduced-motion`. **This library has no `Text`, no `Image` and no `Icon`** — the sheet has no typography component — so there is nothing for that context to attach to, and a skeleton cannot be built out of components that are not here. The shimmer therefore goes on the element this component renders, which wraps the content instead. The property that matters survives: the content is hidden but **still laid out**, so the placeholder's box is the box the real content will occupy, and the page does not move when it arrives. What is lost is one gradient per component; what is gained is that any markup can be skeletonised without the per-component opt-in React Spectrum's own library needed. The context is published anyway, and it is the one part of the React Spectrum mechanism that had to survive, because it is the only way a _consumer's_ component can tell it is inside a placeholder and skip work nobody can see. `Skeleton.stories.tsx`'s `OptIn` story is one. ### The gradient is mixed from the placeholder's own colour The highlight is `color-mix(in oklch, var(--foreground) 12%, var(--muted))`, not a second grey. Every hover and pressed state in this system already derives from its base rather than substituting a colour, and the same rule pays off here: `--foreground` inverts with the theme, so one declaration lightens the dark theme's placeholder and darkens the light theme's. 12% is `TRACK_WASH`'s wash — a step you can see across a card and cannot mistake for a border. The stops sit at 33% and 66% of a gradient that is three times the box's width, which is why a placeholder at rest — the reduced-motion case — shows the flat `--muted` end of it rather than a band parked in the middle of the box. ### `visibility`, not `display` `[&_*]:invisible` takes the subtree out of the picture **and the accessibility tree** while leaving every box exactly where it was. `display: none` would collapse the placeholder to nothing, which is the one thing a skeleton must not do; and hiding the _wrapper_ instead would hide the shimmer as well. ### Three things are not left to the caller - **The subtree is `inert`.** Nothing inside is visible, so nothing inside may be tabbed to, clicked or announced. That is also how React Spectrum disables the form components in a skeleton, without a second prop for a consumer to remember. `Skeleton.browser.test.tsx` presses a button inside one and checks focus does not land. - **The sweep is synchronised across the page.** Every skeleton sets its `startTime` to `0`, React Spectrum's own technique. A CSS keyframe starts when each element mounts, so two placeholders that appeared a second apart are visibly out of step and read as two things loading rather than one screen. `Synchronized` is the story that measures it. - **`prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured**, and what is left is a _still_ placeholder rather than no placeholder: the movement the reader asked to be spared, not the state. ### No element at all once it is loaded With `isLoading={false}` this component renders its children and nothing else — no wrapper to work around, and no `data-slot="skeleton"` in the page. **The root only exists while the placeholder does**, which is worth knowing before writing a test that queries it: the honest assertion while loaded is that it is _absent_, not that it is invisible. `Loaded` is that story. ## Granularity is the caller's Wrap a whole card and it shimmers as one surface; wrap each line and each one shimmers on its own. The second is how a skeleton screen is usually drawn, and it needs no content at all — a bare placeholder is sized entirely by `className`: ```tsx
``` **The wrapper is a block box**, which is what a placeholder surface is: it is the container's width and the content's height. A placeholder that has to sit _inside_ a line of running text therefore does not have a form here — put the bar in a block-level parent, sized as a line, or wrap the line it belongs to. **A placeholder is not a spinner.** A spinner says something specific is happening and is used for one control's pending state (`isPending` on `Button`); a skeleton is used when a _region_ is being fetched and its shape is already known. Using both in the same region says it twice.
